summary: Senator Barrasso has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about energy supply, competition with China and the Senate's schedule for AI bills.

Senator Blunt Rochester has acknowledged that AI could threaten human life. She wrote that even a 1% chance AI could wipe out human life is reason to be "pumping the brakes", and has pressed OpenAI and Anthropic about AI models that act on their own.

Senator Collins has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Asked about warnings that AI could cause human extinction, she said the best path balances AI's promise with its risks, naming consumer protections and critical infrastructure.
Senator Coons has acknowledged that AI poses an existential risk. He has written of "the existential threat posed by AI" and said the level of risk "for us as a species" is accelerating.
Senator Cramer has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The one remark found from him is about the politics of AI regulation.
Senator Durbin has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about testing AI systems, liability for AI companies and protecting children who use chatbots.
Senator Graham has made no statement about AI that we could find. She was appointed in July 2026.
Senator Hagerty has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. He has called AI "an extraordinarily disruptive technology" while saying he is optimistic about its productivity gains.

Senator Heinrich has acknowledged serious risk from AI in general terms, but has not described a catastrophic risk himself. Sharing a warning about AI, he wrote that "this is a real warning and we need to take it seriously".
Senator Husted has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about protecting children from chatbots and the US winning the AI race.

Senator Kaine has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, but not in his own words. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators warns that frontier AI could enable biological weapons and calls the stakes existential. Speaking for himself, he said "we don't need to be just complete doomsdayers about it".

Senator Kelly has acknowledged that AI could threaten human survival. On the Senate floor he said engineers, researchers and company heads are warning of AI "becoming a threat to humanity's very survival", and compared the moment to a cockpit alarm with nobody steering.

Senator Marshall has acknowledged serious risk from AI in general terms, but not catastrophic risk. He has said the biggest threat is to cybersecurity and that he is "not as fearful as some people are of a runaway AI", though "we need to keep our eye on that as well".

Senator Moreno has dismissed warnings of catastrophic risk from AI. In a letter to Anthropic's chief executive he called warnings that AI "could end humanity" alarmist "doomerism". He has said the risks of advanced AI must be addressed, without saying what they are.

Senator Murphy has acknowledged that AI poses an existential risk. He endorsed a warning that AI companies are in "a blind race to build a death machine" and has called coming AI "an existential threat". In 2025 he wrote that AI "isn't going to become omnipotent and evil and murder us all".

Senator Murray has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, and has spoken about AI risk in general terms herself. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators calls AI "a technology that poses an existential threat". In her own words, she has said the president is "totally wrong" to call AI risks a hoax.

Senator Schiff has acknowledged that AI could threaten humanity. He has said he has been "hearing about the existential threat to humankind for years" from people who build AI, and has called for formal coordination with China on the most capable models.

Senator Sullivan has acknowledged serious risk from AI in general terms, but not catastrophic risk. He has said "clear safeguards around the highest-risk AI technologies" are needed, without naming the risks; his other statements are about beating China in the AI race.

Senator Thune has acknowledged serious risk from advanced AI in general terms, but has not described it as catastrophic in his own words. He has said the more advanced threats are real and should be mitigated without stifling innovation, and also that there is "a lot of hyperbole" around the issue.
Senator Wicker has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about winning the AI race with China, "light touch" regulation and the local costs of data centers.
Senator-elect Moore has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The only relevant statement found is a post about data center electricity bills and staying ahead in technology.
Senator-elect Stratton has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her one detailed statement on AI, in a candidate questionnaire, is about jobs, fairness and privacy.
Senator-elect Turek has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The only relevant statements found are debate remarks about not ceding ground to China on AI and regulating data centers.
Senator-elect Hamilton has acknowledged that AI could threaten the human race. In a debate exchange about AI regulation he said "This is a potential existential threat to the human race".
Senator-elect Barr has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His posts and bills on AI are about powering data centers and winning the AI race with China.

Senator-elect Letlow has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her posts on AI promote data center investment in her home state of Louisiana and say data centers should pay their own energy costs.
Senator-elect Jackson has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His posts on AI are about data centers, AI-powered surveillance and harms to jobs and children.

Senator-elect El-Sayed has acknowledged that AI could threaten humanity's survival. He has said AI could develop "to the point that it poses an existential threat to humanity", and has called for a pause, a treaty with China and a ban on AI that improves itself.
Senator-elect Flanagan has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. In a debate she said "we have to be very clear that there are catastrophic risks that AI poses".
Senator-elect Alme has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The only AI-relevant statements he has made are about data center construction in his home state of Montana.

Senator-elect Pappas has acknowledged that AI could threaten humanity. In a radio interview he said people who build AI are warning of "potentially a 10% chance that this could obliterate humanity", and asked "Who wants to take that chance?"
Senator-elect Cooper has acknowledged the risk of humans losing control of AI. He called reports of "humans losing control of AI" alarming and said the warnings of AI company heads should be heeded.

Senator-elect Brown has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The only AI-relevant statements he has made are campaign criticism of data center tax breaks and electricity costs in his home state of Ohio.
Senator-elect Hern has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His posts on AI promote American leadership in AI and a law against non-consensual explicit AI images.

Senator-elect Andrews has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. She has called for regulating AI tools that can discriminate, and for a two-year halt to new data centers in South Carolina over energy costs.
Senator-elect Talarico has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about data center costs and tax deals, and keeping advanced chips from adversaries.
Senator-elect Hageman has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her statements and bills on AI are about government censorship through AI and the use of AI in courts.

Senator Alsobrooks has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, but not in her own words. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators calls AI "a technology that poses an existential threat". Her own statements on AI are about opportunity, jobs and workforce training.
Senator Armstrong has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about faster permitting, the power grid and data centers, which he ties to America leading in AI.

Senator Baldwin has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. She said Wisconsinites want assurance that AI "will not become capable of operating beyond human control", and called for action to "pump the brakes on these frontier models".

Senator Banks has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. In a letter to the administration he wrote that there are unresolved questions about whether we have "the ability to keep powerful AI systems under our control", especially as companies pursue superintelligence.

Senator Bennet has acknowledged that AI could threaten human survival. He said warnings from people inside AI companies that "humanity could be destroyed by AI" must be listened to, and proposed a regulator able to act against models that could threaten "the extinction of humanity".

Senator Blackburn has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, through a bill she drafted rather than in her own remarks. Her office's summary of the bill says large developers would have to "manage and mitigate catastrophic risk"; her own statements are about children, creators and one federal rulebook.

Senator Booker has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. In a Senate floor speech he said "we must protect against potentially catastrophic harms", citing warnings about dangerous biological or cyber capabilities and systems humans cannot reliably predict or control.

Senator Boozman has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The one statement found, in a letter about electricity supply, says the nation needs more power to "win the Artificial Intelligence race"; Boozman's other mentions of AI treat it as a practical tool.

Senator Britt has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her statements on AI are about protecting children from chatbots, transparency from AI companies and who pays for data center electricity.

Senator Budd has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. Introducing a bill, he said "we may face the real prospect of AI-generated threats like biological or chemical weapons". He has also said AI development need not slow down, because China is not slowing down.

Senator Cantwell has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, and has spoken about catastrophic risk herself. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators calls AI "a technology that poses an existential threat". In her own words, she has said dangers such as "autonomous cyberattacks and biological weapons" are "no longer theoretical".
Senator Capito has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her statements on AI are about voluntary guidelines for checking AI systems, AI-enabled fraud and scams, and data centers.

Senator Cassidy has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. In a series of posts summarising an article on governing AI, he wrote that "AI could cause harm through the digital systems civilization depends upon" and that humans would not control a superintelligence: "trust is not control".

Senator Cornyn has dismissed warnings of catastrophic risk from AI. Asked about Bill Gates's warning that AI could kill a billion people, he called it "incredibly irresponsible" and said "he's fearmongering".
Senator Cotton has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about competition with China, keeping advanced AI chips from adversaries, Chinese AI models and data centers.

Senator Crapo has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The one statement found from him is about staying competitive in AI and who pays for the electricity infrastructure that data centers need.

Senator Curtis has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a catastrophic outcome. In a joint statement he said AI technologies should "remain fully under human control" and that "Congress must ensure necessary safeguards are in place".

Senator Daines has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. He said there are "downside risks, you know, bio-terrorism, other things that we need to be very concerned about". In the same interview he accused some colleagues warning about AI of "creating hysteria".

Senator Duckworth has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, but not in her own words. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators calls AI "a technology that poses an existential threat". Speaking for herself, she has said "we must remain the master of the technology and not the other way around".

Senator Ernst has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. She has called for guardrails so that AI systems "cannot go rogue or be misused by our adversaries", without naming a consequence, and has argued against pausing AI development because China would not pause.

Senator Fetterman has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. In an op-ed written with another senator he cited "the growing dangers of biological, cyber, and nuclear attacks" and called for accountability if an AI system causes catastrophic harm. He has also said he rejects "hyperbole over data centers or AI doomsdaying".

Senator Fischer has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her statements on AI are about communications networks, economic benefits, competition with other countries and who pays for the electricity that data centers use.

Senator Gallego has acknowledged that AI could threaten human survival. In a television interview he said "humanity could be totally gone within a couple of years", and he has said that earlier technology "could not make a decision to kill us".

Senator Gillibrand has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a specific catastrophe. Speaking about military use of AI, she said removing guardrails "guarantees a future of catastrophic harm", and she co-signed a letter backing action to "mitigate risks posed by misalignment in the models themselves".

Senator Grassley has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about protecting whistleblowers at AI companies, Chinese espionage against American AI companies, judges using AI to draft court orders, and data center energy costs.

Senator Hassan has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her statements on AI are about research to make AI "harder to manipulate and easier to predict", cyberattacks by foreign adversaries using autonomous AI systems, and AI-enabled scams.

Senator Hickenlooper has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. In a letter to President Trump he wrote that AI systems "rapidly become more powerful and potentially uncontrollable" and warned of "consequences both profound and irreversible".

Senator Hirono has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, but not in her own words. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators calls AI "a technology that poses an existential threat" and says "the stakes are existential". Her own statements on AI are about energy bills and harms from chatbots.

Senator Hoeven has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Asked about a warning that AI could cause a billion deaths, he said the US needs to stay ahead of adversaries like China, "but we need to do it safely".

Senator Van Hollen has acknowledged that AI could threaten humanity. He led the September 2026 letter from 17 senators that calls AI "a technology that poses an existential threat", and in his own statement promised to keep pressing for guardrails "to protect humanity from the threat of unregulated AI development".

Senator Hyde-Smith has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The one remark found from her mentions AI in passing as a military research capability; her posts are about an AI company expansion, data centers and electricity rates, and competition with China.

Senator Johnson has acknowledged that AI could threaten human survival. In an interview he said he is "concerned about out-of-control AI" and wants basic laws so that it does not "destroy the human race". Asked later about similar warnings from AI company insiders, he said "There's fear-mongering. I'm not buying it".

Senator Justice has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about protecting older people who use chatbots, disclosing when AI is used in customer service calls, and using West Virginia coal and gas to power AI.

Senator Kennedy has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. On the Senate floor he said that if there is "even a 1% chance" an AI model could "become an independent species" that humans cannot control, "we ought to take it seriously"; his bill would require a shutdown mechanism in advanced AI models.

Senator Kim has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. He has written of "the potentially catastrophic threat AI poses to our national security", including AI helping someone build a bioweapon, and has said action is needed "to ensure that humans remain in control of this technology".

Senator King has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. In a letter to the Treasury Secretary he wrote of "the potentially catastrophic implications of uncontrolled AI development" and urged AI safety talks with China. He has also called the threat from AI "damn serious".

Senator Klobuchar has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a catastrophic outcome. While negotiating an AI safety bill, she said the release of "dangerous models, including those that evade the control of their developers" cannot be allowed.

Senator Lankford has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a catastrophic outcome. He co-signed a letter to AI companies citing "potential risks involving public safety and national security" from more capable models; his own statements are about transparency for families, talks with China, and AI and faith.

Senator Lee has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about competition with China, which he and other senators called "our main competitor in the race for AI dominance", along with automated pricing by companies and the electricity demand of data centers.

Senator Luján has acknowledged existential risk from AI. In his own letter to Senate leaders he wrote that leaders at top AI laboratories suggest "a 10% to 20% chance of existential risks", and he signed the September 2026 letter of 17 senators calling AI "a technology that poses an existential threat".

Senator Lummis has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her bill on AI liability says AI systems "may significantly impact the future of human civilization" without naming a harm; her other statements are about powering data centers and beating China in AI.

Senator Markey has acknowledged existential risk from AI. He wrote that Congress must "act to stop existential threats to our future", and in a letter with a House colleague urged steps to ensure AI does not cause "a preventable nuclear disaster".

Senator Cortez Masto has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, and has spoken about AI risk in general terms herself. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators names dangers that threaten "humanity writ large". In her own words, she has said "the safety risks for Americans are also increasing every day".

Senator McConnell has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The statements found welcome the choice of Paducah, Kentucky to host "new AI infrastructure" and mention autonomous systems in passing in a speech about defense spending.

Senator McCormick has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. He has written of "the growing dangers of biological, cyber, and nuclear attacks" and of powerful AI that "causes catastrophic harm". He has also dismissed as "hysterical" the claims "that AI will kill us all".

Senator Merkley has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, but not in his own words. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators calls AI "a technology that poses an existential threat". His own statements are about AI disinformation in elections and harm from AI "in the wrong hands".

Senator Moody has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. Her statements on AI are about scams against seniors, deepfakes, children's safety and data center electricity costs; in that context she said Congress must "ensure it never gets out of control".

Senator Moran has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. His statements on AI are about helping small businesses use it and about AI education, so that the next generation "can utilize its full potential".

Senator Murkowski has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The one remark found in her own words is about AI-enabled toys and their effect on the "physical, mental, and emotional development of our children".

Senator Ossoff has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. In a letter to the White House he wrote that malicious actors could use AI "to develop potentially dangerous pathogens and biological weapons", and he has called for inspectors in frontier labs and "an AI treaty".

Senator Padilla has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, and has spoken about biological weapons risks himself. The September 2026 letter from 17 senators says "the stakes are existential". Describing it, he cited "biological weapons risks", and he has asked the FBI about "AI agents going rogue".

Senator Paul has dismissed warnings of catastrophic risk from AI. He wrote that "many AI doomers" want liability protections and are "begging the government to get involved", adding "Don't be fooled!" His other statements argue against regulating AI in haste.

Senator Peters has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a catastrophic outcome. He has said powerful AI models "are already presenting real risks and challenges to our national security" and that the federal government is "behind the curve".

Senator Reed has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a catastrophic outcome. He has said guardrails are essential to protecting "people, our economy, and humanity itself", and that officials should heed industry warnings that AI "may be evolving at an unsafe pace".

Senator Ricketts has not acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI. The statements found are about winning the AI competition with China, limits on sales of AI chips to Beijing and the cost of data centers, including that a China "dominant in AI is very bad for the United States".

Senator Risch has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a catastrophic outcome. Introducing a bill on testing AI systems, he said "we must be cognizant of bad actors and potential threats to privacy and national security".

Senator Rosen has acknowledged that AI could threaten humanity. She wrote that "The AI industry itself says that this technology is a threat to humanity" and said AI could "cause catastrophic damages" without guardrails. She also signed the September 2026 letter of 17 senators saying "the stakes are existential".

Senator Rounds has acknowledged serious risks from AI in general terms, without naming a catastrophic outcome. In a letter with another senator he called for testing advanced AI models for "serious national-security risks", including "biological and chemical threats"; his own remarks oppose slowing AI research because China would take the lead.

Senator Schatz has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. Asked about warnings that AI could end humanity, he said "I think the risk is acute" and that he is "not really willing to tolerate that level of catastrophic risk".

Senator Schmitt has dismissed warnings of catastrophic risk from AI. He has described concern about AI as a panic, writing of "the people selling the panic" who "stand to gain from Washington’s response". His other statements are about the AI race with China and having one national set of AI rules.

Senator Schumer has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. On the Senate floor he spoke of "real concerns of the potential catastrophic risks of unchecked AI" and of "AI going rogue" without human control.

Senator Smith has acknowledged existential risk from AI by signing a letter, and has spoken about AI dangers in general terms herself. Senator Warner has acknowledged catastrophic risk from AI, without describing it as a threat of extinction. Asked whether AI poses an imminent existential threat, he said "I don't believe imminent existential threat, but potentially catastrophic threat, yes." He has also said talk of human extinction is "over the top".

She has also called for an immediate pause on the development of advanced AI.
